common_name: Barbara Jackman Clematis (Purple-Blue Large-Flowered Clematis with Red-Purple Bar)

planting.note: A pruning group two cultivar; only lightly tidy old wood in late winter, since the main flush comes from buds set the previous season.

directions: Introduced in 1952 and still one of the most recognizable early-flowering hybrids, this cultivar opens violet-blue, six- to eight-sepaled blooms 6 to 8 inches across, each marked with a bold carmine-red central bar that fades as the flower ages. It flowers first in late spring on the previous year's wood, then produces a lighter second flush on new growth in late summer, so pruning should stay light in late winter, removing only dead or damaged stems. Give it a fence, arbor, or obelisk to climb and keep the root zone shaded and cool with mulch or a low companion planting while the vine reaches into full sun. Its tolerance of a wide range of soils and reliable, early color have kept it a mainstay of clematis collections for decades.

common_name: Marie Boisselot Clematis (Classic Large White Clematis)

planting.note: Pruning group two; remove only dead or weak stems in late winter to preserve the heavy early-summer bloom set on old wood.

directions: Bred in France in 1885 and sold in some catalogs under the synonym 'Madame Le Coultre', this long-standing favorite produces enormous, pure white, overlapping-sepaled flowers 6 to 8 inches across with contrasting cream stamens, opening from early summer and often repeating lightly into fall. Because most of its bloom comes from buds formed the previous season, prune only to remove dead or damaged wood in late winter rather than cutting the vine back hard. Provide a sturdy trellis, pergola post, or fence, keeping the roots cool and shaded beneath mulch or low underplanting while the foliage climbs into full sun. Its vigor, cold hardiness, and dependable, large-scale flowers have made it one of the most widely planted white large-flowered clematis for well over a century.

planting.note: Pruning group three; flowers entirely on new growth, so cut the whole vine back to about a foot from the ground each late winter.

directions: One of the oldest named viticella selections still in commerce, dating to the late nineteenth century, this cultivar bears small, nodding, four-sepaled flowers in a deep wine-red that darken further as they age, produced in great abundance from midsummer into fall. As with other viticella types, its resistance to clematis wilt and forgiving hard-pruning regime make it an easy, reliable choice for scrambling through an early-blooming shrub or covering a fence quickly each season. Keep the root zone mulched and shaded while the vine climbs into full sun, and water regularly through dry spells in the first couple of establishment years. Its small flower size and airy habit suit it to weaving through roses or other climbers rather than standing alone as a specimen.

common_name: Purpurea Plena Elegans Clematis (Double Purple-Red Viticella Clematis)

planting.note: Pruning group three; blooms only on new wood, so cut all stems back hard to a strong bud pair near the base each late winter.

directions: Recorded in cultivation since at least 1899, this historic viticella selection produces fully double, rosette-shaped flowers in dusky purple-red, packed with narrow, slightly twisted sepals that give the bloom a shaggy pompom appearance quite unlike the flat, single flowers of most viticella cultivars. It flowers prolifically on new growth from midsummer into fall, so the entire vine can be cut back hard to about a foot from the ground each late winter, avoiding the guesswork required by old-wood, large-flowered types. Give it a fence, obelisk, or shrub to scramble through, and keep the roots cool and shaded with mulch while the vine reaches into full sun. Its viticella parentage also lends good resistance to clematis wilt, making it a dependable and unusual addition to a mixed-cultivar collection.

common_name: Gravetye Beauty Clematis (Scarlet Tulip-Form Texensis Clematis)

planting.note: Pruning group three; blooms on new growth, so cut the vine back hard to a foot or so above the ground each late winter.

directions: Raised by the noted garden writer William Robinson at Gravetye Manor around 1900, this texensis hybrid produces nodding, tulip-shaped flowers in glowing scarlet-crimson with recurved petal tips, opening from midsummer into fall on a wiry, more restrained vine than the large-flowered hybrids. Grow it up a narrow obelisk, wire trellis, or through a small shrub, keeping the roots cool and shaded beneath mulch or low companion plants while the top growth flowers in full sun. Like other Texas-parentage cultivars, it tolerates heat and dry spells better than most large-flowered clematis, making it a good choice for warmer or drier gardens. Because it flowers entirely on new wood, cut the whole vine back hard each late winter to renew vigor and maximize bloom.

common_name: Alionushka Clematis (Non-Vining Nodding Pink Herbaceous Clematis)

planting.note: Flowers on new growth; cut the whole plant back to a low bud pair in late winter to keep it tidy and encourage the strongest bloom.

directions: Bred by Russian hybridizer Mikhail Beskaravainyi and introduced in the 1980s from integrifolia parentage, this cultivar forms a lax, semi-shrubby clump rather than a true climber, producing nodding, bell-shaped, dusky rose-pink flowers with gently twisted, recurved petal tips over a long summer season. Its sprawling habit works well woven through a low shrub or trained lightly up a short obelisk, or simply left to spill across the front of a mixed border without any climbing support. Because it flowers entirely on new growth, cutting the whole plant back to a few inches in late winter keeps it compact and encourages the fullest flush the following summer. Water regularly through the growing season and mulch to keep the roots cool, since even non-climbing clematis types prefer a shaded root run.
